cases.title: Greece Memorandum Pension Cuts
cases.point: Syntagma Square, opposite parliament, where retired pharmacist Dimitris Christoulas died on 4 April 2012 (the pension cuts were national)

lenders.name: Euro-area countries
lenders.role: Pledged €80 billion in bilateral loans of the €110 billion May 2010 package (IMF Press Release 10/176). Act 4046/2012 approved the draft loan agreements with the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF) for the second programme and a draft Memorandum of Understanding between Greece, the European Commission and the Bank of Greece (Greek government submissions to the European Committee of Social Rights).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Lent about €30 billion of the May 2010 package through a three-year Stand-By Arrangement; it said the 2010 measures 'involve a reduction of public sector wages and pension outlays' (IMF Press Release 10/176). The Greek government told the Committee the support mechanism was set up by the European Commission, the European Central Bank and the IMF.

lenders.name: European Commission and European Central Bank
lenders.role: Set up and monitored the support mechanism with the IMF (the 'Troika'), according to the Greek government (European Committee of Social Rights decision, 2012). The ECB did not itself lend.

cases.conditions: Act 3845 of 6 May 2010 put in place the support mechanism of the euro-area countries and the IMF and annexed the Memoranda setting out a programme of fiscal and structural measures; the Greek government said keeping to the Memoranda timetable was 'a prerequisite for the disbursement of loan installments'. Before the Committee, the government said the pension cuts were part of that programme. The pension measures it listed: a 'solidarity contribution' of 3% to 14% on main pensions above €1,400 a month, from 1 August 2010 (Act 3863/2010); a further 6% to 10% for pensioners under 60 with pensions above €1,700, from 1 August 2011 (Act 3986/2011); from 1 November 2011, a 40% cut on the part above €1,000 for pensioners under 55 and 20% on the part above €1,200 for those over 55 (Act 4024/2011); and a 12% cut on the part above €1,300, from 1 January 2012 (Act 4051/2012). Christmas, Easter and summer bonuses became fixed sums of €400, €200 and €200, paid only to pensioners aged 60 or over with pensions of up to €2,500 a month (Acts 3845/2010 and 4038/2012). (Greek government submissions, September 2012.)
cases.community: Pensioners lost part of their monthly pensions under each law. The pensioners' federation told the Committee that pensions had been cut six times, that auxiliary pensions fell by about 30% and pensions of early retirees by about half, and that a change to the solidarity benefit cut off between 20,000 and 50,000 people. The government did not contest this account, and the Committee found the combined cuts were 'bound to bring about a significant degradation' of many pensioners' living standards, and that they risked impoverishing a large part of the population (European Committee of Social Rights). On 4 April 2012 Dimitris Christoulas, a 77-year-old retired pharmacist, shot himself in Syntagma Square. A note found on him, published by Greek media, said the government had made it impossible to survive on a pension he had paid into for 35 years; police did not confirm the note was genuine (AP). AP wrote that Greece had imposed pension and salary cuts to secure international rescue loans.
cases.suppression: After Christoulas's death, some 1,500 people protested at the square; youths threw rocks and petrol bombs and riot police fired tear gas and flash grenades. Authorities reported no injuries or arrests (AP; Al Jazeera).
cases.killed_note: Not counted: Dimitris Christoulas took his own life; his note tied it to his pension (AP, RNZ, Al Jazeera).
cases.outcome: On 7 December 2012 the European Committee of Social Rights unanimously found that the cumulative effect of the pension cuts in twelve laws from 2010 to 2012, including Acts 3845/2010, 3863/2010, 4024/2011 and 4051/2012, violated Article 12§3 (right to social security) of the European Social Charter (complaint 76/2012, IKA-ETAM v. Greece). It said the government had not carried out even minimal study of the effects on vulnerable groups or discussed them with pensioners' organisations, and that Greece's loan obligations to the EU institutions and the IMF did not remove the laws from the Charter's reach. It found the holiday-bonus cuts did not in themselves breach the Charter. The decision was notified on 20 December 2012, and the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers adopted Resolution ResChS(2014)7 on 2 July 2014 (Council of Europe).

cases.confidence_note: The link to the loans rests on the Greek government's own account to the Committee, that the pension cuts were part of the Memoranda programme on which each loan payment depended, and on the IMF's 2010 statement that the programme cut pension outlays. The government denied any breach of the Charter and said the measures exempted the most vulnerable groups. The euro-area countries lent about three-quarters of the 2010 money, so the measures were not the IMF's alone. The suicide note was published by Greek media; police did not confirm it.

lvwhy.cuts: Pensions above set thresholds were cut in four laws from 2010 to 2012 under the Memoranda programme tied to the loans.
